title: Excess Dissolved Inorganic Carbon (eDIC) as a Simplifying Metric for Riverine Carbonate Chemistry
content:
Abstract

We develop a new simplifying metric, “excess DIC” (eDIC), dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) minus alkalinity (Alk), to gain insight into the drivers of spatial and temporal variability in riverine pCO2, [H+], and CaCO3 saturation state. [eDIC] is insensitive to most open-system weathering reactions and well-approximated by [CO2]–[CO3 2–] in a wide variety of environments and by [CO2] in a more restricted but still common set of environments (low to moderate pH). eDIC is used to analyze historical carbonate chemistry data of rivers draining the Chesapeake Bay Watershed. Annual-mean pCO2 and [H+] vary by factors of 3.9 and 27, respectively, across the rivers, but are well-explained by [eDIC], as are the mean annual cycles of these variables after including effects of temperature on equilibrium constants. Even larger spatial and seasonal variability in CaCO3 saturation state is found, mainly driven by alkalinity, with smaller contributions from eDIC and temperature. [eDIC] generally increases with increasing streamflow, is lower in the summer, and has annual means that increase with the fraction of streamflow from overland flow and decrease with the amount of carbonate rock and soil in the watershed. These patterns are consistent with [eDIC] decreasing with depth in the soil column as a result of a transition from open-system to closed-system weathering. [Alk]–[DIC] has seen increasing use in oceanography and we demonstrate here that its negative—excess DIC—shows promise for understanding rivers, particularly when compared to the more-frequently used [DIC]/[Alk] ratio.
